The comparative churn rate is the useful number: CAIO turnover/creation is ~4x CDO. Also note the base is small: ~1,180 CAIOs worldwide is a thin market for a dedicated programme.

skill: AI governance job postings - volume and seniority
metric: The analysis examined 1,997 US job postings for AI governance roles; Manager roles: 28%, Senior IC: 24%, Mid-level IC: 17%, Director: 12%, Junior IC: 8%, Principal IC: 5%; 56% of postings originate from organizations with 10,000+ employees; enterprises above 1,000 headcount represent 77% of the market
note: 1,997 postings - say so when citing. 40% of postings are Manager or Director level, and the buyer is overwhelmingly the large enterprise. This is the best posting-level evidence for an AI governance exec-ed offer.

skill: Capabilities named in AI governance postings
source: Axial Search, 'The State of the AI Governance Job Market in 2026'
metric: Observability platforms: 41% of postings; Python: 28%; NIST frameworks: 27%; Governance discipline ranks highest, followed by AI literacy. Use case selection and value framing follow next, then hands-on execution, with adoption-driving ranked lowest; Senior level or above: 73% of all postings; Median salary: $169,000
note: Same 1,997-posting dataset. The capability ranking is the finding: employers want governance discipline plus AI literacy plus use-case selection and value framing - which is precisely an exec-ed curriculum, not a technical one. But 41% also demand model observability tooling, which no exec ed programme teaches. SUPPLY GAP.

skill: Organisations working on AI governance
metric: 77% of surveyed organizations are currently working on AI governance; ~90% of organizations already using AI; Only 1.5% (10 of 671 respondents) reported they will not need additional staff in the next 12 months; primary responsibility sits with Privacy 22%, Legal and compliance 22%, IT 17%, Data governance 10%
note: Survey, so weaker than postings. Note where the function sits: privacy and legal own AI governance in 44% of organisations - the audience for an AI governance programme is the GC/CPO/CRO, not the CTO.

skill: AI job titles spreading outside tech occupations in Europe
metric: Germany: 59% of AI-labelled titles outside tech; Netherlands 58%; France 54%; UK 54%; Spain 36%. AI-labelled job titles Q1 2026 vs Q1 2022: Germany 288 vs 72, UK 160 vs 61, France 138 vs 35, Netherlands 84 vs 21, Spain 81 vs 8. Share of AI-labelled titles in all postings Q1 2026: Germany 4.2% (was 0.8% in 2022), France 3.3%, UK 2.7%, Spain 2.3%, Netherlands 2.2%
note: Best European behavioural evidence in this pull. Germany is the European leader and has quintupled in four years. Non-tech examples cited: sales, HR, legal services, customer support, administrative.

skill: AI adoption and total job postings
source: Federal Reserve FEDS Notes, "AI Adoption and Firms' Job-Posting Behavior"
metric: there is no evidence thus far that industries with higher levels of AI adoption are posting fewer jobs; firm-level coefficients positive and significant at short lags (0.082*** at 1-month) declining to -0.0002 at 12 months. Data: Lightcast postings Sept 2023-Nov 2025 and Census BTOS; 7.3 million firm-month records across 1.05 million firms
note: CONTRADICTION SIGNAL. The most rigorous source in this pull finds no aggregate job destruction from AI adoption through Nov 2025. This undercuts programmes sold on 'leading through AI-driven workforce disruption' as an urgent 2027 need, though the 12-month coefficient turning to zero hints the short-run boost fades.

skill: India GCC scale
source: Zinnov and NASSCOM, India GCC Landscape 2026, via Flexiple
metric: GCC Count: 2,117 across 3,728 individual centres; Employment: 2.36 million people; Revenue: $98.4 billion; 32% increase since FY2021; "200+ new GCCs entered India between 2024-early 2026"; "40% of all India office leasing driven by GCC demand in 2025"; NASSCOM projects headcount exceeding 2.5 million by 2030
note: Secondary aggregation of Zinnov/NASSCOM - not the primary report. 2,117 GCCs each needing a site leader is a concrete addressable market for a GCC-leadership programme.

skill: GCC hiring momentum India
metric: GCC hiring remained steady (-1%) at the national level, but Southern markets continued to outperform. Chennai led with 19% YOY growth in June, followed by Hyderabad at 15%
note: CONTRADICTION SIGNAL. GCC white-collar postings are flat nationally (-1%) even as the GCC count grows - the growth is in centre count and location shift, not aggregate hiring. Tempers the GCC-boom narrative.

skill: AI/ML role growth India and senior-experience hiring
metric: AI/ML roles continued their strong run, posting 25% YOY growth in June; White-collar hiring grew +6% in June, with the Naukri JobSpeak Index reaching 3027. Experience-level growth: 4-7 years 2%, 8-12 years 7%, 13-16 years 12%, 16+ years 9%
note: Key seniority finding: in India the 13-16 year band is growing fastest (12%), well above the 4-7 year band (2%). Demand is skewing senior - directly relevant to exec-ed pricing and positioning.

skill: Workflow automation / agentic workflow design for managers
source: LinkedIn Skills on the Rise 2026 (India) via Storyboard18

note: PARTIAL GAP. T03.S03.P05 (Automation, RPA, process digitisation) and T03.S01.P03 (Agentic AI) each cover half. The posting-level concept - a manager redesigning a workflow around AI agents - straddles both.

skill: AI literacy obligation (EU AI Act Article 4)
metric: Employers must "take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy"; obligation applies to "staff - and any other person dealing with AI systems on their behalf", extending to "contractors, service providers and customers". Application date 2 February 2025; enforcement date 3 August 2026.
note: The only EU-wide legal mandate to TRAIN people on AI. Binds every provider and deployer, not just tech firms. Audience is all staff, so the executive-education slice is the leadership-level module (what the board/ExCo must understand), not the whole obligation. Enforcement machinery live from Aug 2026 means budget releases 2026-2028.

skill: EU AI Act high-risk obligations deferred by Digital Omnibus
metric: Annex III high-risk deadline moved from 2 August 2026 to "2 December 2027"; Annex I (regulated products) from 2 August 2027 to "2 August 2028"; AI regulatory sandboxes to "2 August 2027". Article 4 AI literacy "retained but softened".
note: Critical for demand timing: the compliance cliff did NOT disappear, it moved INTO the 2027-2031 study window. Peak preparation demand now falls in 2027 (Dec 2027 deadline) rather than 2026. Article 4 survived the simplification round - the training obligation is the part the EU chose not to cut.

skill: Digital Omnibus in force; AI Act penalties unchanged
metric: Regulation "entered into force on 27 July 2026" following Official Journal publication on 24 July 2026. Penalties "remain unchanged", maximum "EUR 35 million or 7 percent of global annual turnover". Annex III high-risk: "2 December 2027"; Annex I: "2 August 2028"; Article 50(2) watermarking: "2 December 2026".
note: Answers the 'is this demand real' question: the omnibus is law, the delay is settled, and the penalty ceiling was not touched. A 7%-of-turnover exposure with a fixed Dec-2027 date is the strongest executive-attention driver in this whole dataset.

skill: Board obligations under the EU AI Act
metric: "Boards may delegate operational work, but not accountability." "Human oversight is not satisfied by nominal review processes. It requires that the humans responsible for oversight have the authority, information, and practical ability to override system outputs when necessary." Fines up to "EUR 35 million or 7% of global turnover".
note: This is the sharpest board-level hook: Article 14/26 human oversight is a competence requirement, not a process requirement. Creates genuine board-programme demand (T08.S01.P04, T03.S02.P05). Note the article's timeline predates/ignores the omnibus deferral - it still says Aug 2026 for high-risk, which is now wrong; treat its dates as unreliable, its governance reasoning as usable.

skill: AI in HR/employment classified high-risk (Annex III point 4)
metric: High-risk classification covers AI used for "recruitment, candidate selection, performance evaluation, task allocation, monitoring of workers, and decisions on promotion or termination". Omnibus defers "the high-risk compliance deadline from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027".
note: Puts the CHRO squarely in scope of the AI Act by Dec 2027. Maps to T07.S03.P02 (AI in HR) and T07.S01.P02 (CHRO). This is a named, dated obligation on a specific C-suite role - stronger than generic 'AI for HR' demand. Pub date on the page was not clearly stated; treat as 2026.

skill: CSRD post-Omnibus scope and first reporting year
metric: From FY 2027 reporting, CSRD applies to EU companies with "over 1,000 employees" and net turnover exceeding "EUR450m", and non-EU companies with "over EUR450m turnover in the EU". Approximately 42,000 companies (90% of originally planned scope) fall out of scope. Second/third wave reporting begins FY 2027 (due 2028); non-EU companies FY 2028 due 2029.
note: The single biggest negative finding in this batch. CSRD demand did not grow - it shrank by ~90% of the addressable population. Whatever ESG-reporting programme demand existed in 2024 forecasts should be marked down hard for Europe. The remaining audience is large-cap only, and is a controller/CSO audience more than a board audience.

skill: CSRD Omnibus thresholds - contradictory figures
metric: Companies with "over 1,750 employees and EUR450 million net turnover". Under CS3D the European Parliament removed Article 22 entirely, which "relates to the adoption of climate transition plans".
note: CONTRADICTION with REG006: Norton Rose (Nov 2025, Parliament position) says 1,750 employees; Commonwealth Climate Law (Mar 2026, post-trilogue) says 1,000. The 1,000 figure is the later and more likely final one, but the disagreement is itself evidence that scope was volatile through 2026. Separately: deletion of CS3D Article 22 removes the mandatory climate transition plan duty - that kills a large chunk of assumed 'net-zero transition planning' executive demand in Europe (T10.S01.P02).

skill: BRSR Core reasonable assurance glide path (India)
metric: "FY2023-24: Top 150 listed entities by market capitalisation; FY2024-25: Top 250 listed entities; FY2025-26: Top 500 listed entities; FY2026-27: Top 1,000 listed entities." Framework introduced via SEBI's "July 12, 2023 circular".
note: India moves the opposite way to Europe: scope WIDENS to the top 1,000 listed entities from FY2026-27, i.e. reporting through 2027-28. But the audience is the sustainability/finance controller and the assurance provider, not the CEO. Classify as specialist demand with a thin board-oversight layer (audit committee sign-off), NOT mainstream executive education.

skill: SEBI value chain ESG disclosure made voluntary
metric: Value chain ESG disclosures deferred to "FY 2025-2026" with assessment/assurance starting "FY 2026-2027"; value chain disclosures shifted to a "voluntary basis"; scope refined to partners accounting for "2% or more" of purchases/sales or covering "75% of their total purchases and sales".
note: SEBI eased rather than tightened. A voluntary obligation does not force training spend. Downgrade any 'supply chain ESG for executives' demand thesis in India to discretionary.

skill: ISSB IFRS S1/S2 jurisdictional adoption
metric: Mandatory adopters: Australia "Group 1 entities (the largest reporters) from FY 2024-25"; Hong Kong FY 2025; Singapore FY 2025; UK FY 2025; Brazil FY 2026; Japan first wave "companies with market cap above JPY 3 trillion" in FY 2027. On India: "No formal adoption timeline has been set".
note: ISSB is the real growth vector for sustainability reporting demand 2027-2031, not CSRD. Japan FY2027 is the largest single new cohort in the study window. India has NO ISSB mandate - so an India-sold ISSB programme is anticipatory, not compliance-driven. Tracker covers only 16 jurisdictions; treat coverage as partial.

skill: DPDP Rules 2025 phased compliance dates (India)
metric: "Phase 2 (12 months/November 13, 2026): Consent Manager framework activation. Phase 3 (18 months/May 13, 2027): Core operational obligations become enforceable." Significant Data Fiduciaries must make "Mandatory appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) based in India", conduct "Mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) every 12 months" and engage "an independent data auditor for yearly compliance checks". Penalty "up to Rs 250 crore for a single instance of failure".
note: Hard date inside the window: 13 May 2027. The Rs 250 crore ceiling makes this a board risk item, but the capability it demands (DPO, DPIA, audit) is specialist. Executive-education demand is narrow: a board/audit-committee briefing plus a CXO accountability module. Do not build a full DPDP programme for general managers.

skill: RBI FREE-AI framework - board and C-suite AI literacy
metric: Framework released 13 August 2025. Recommends "board approved AI policies within financial institutions" and urges "capacity building within regulated entities and regulatory bodies, particularly at the board and C-suite levels, to ensure AI literacy and readiness". 26 recommendations across six pillars (Infrastructure, Policy, Capacity, Governance, Protection, Assurance) and 7 sutras.
note: STRONGEST India signal in this dataset for executive AI education. A regulator has named board-and-C-suite AI literacy as a recommendation, with Capacity as one of six pillars. It is recommendation not binding direction as at Sep 2026, so it creates a strong nudge rather than a compliance deadline - but RBI recommendations of this kind typically harden into Master Directions within 2-3 years, i.e. inside the window. Maps to T03.S02.P05 and T13.S01.P01.

skill: RBI draft guidance on model risk management covers AI/ML
metric: Draft released June 2026 for public consultation. Covers "commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, cooperative banks, Regional Rural Banks, All India Financial Institutions, Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), and Credit Information Companies (CICs)" and explicitly encompasses "artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), statistical models, and other analytical models". Boards must "Approve model governance policies", "Define risk appetite", "Periodically review model inventory", "Ensure adequate resources for validation" and "Monitor material model failures".
note: India is going the opposite way to the US on model risk (see REG014). Board duties are explicit and AI/ML is in scope. Final direction likely 2027 - a dated obligation for bank and NBFC boards. Good fit for a BFSI board programme (T13.S01.P01 + T03.S02.P02).

skill: US interagency model risk management guidance revised - board role reduced, genAI excluded
metric: Revised guidance issued 17 April 2026, superseding the 2011 guidance. The agencies "explicitly excluded generative and agentic AI models from the guidance's scope because these technologies are 'novel and rapidly evolving'". The guidance states "Model risk management benefits from clear roles and responsibilities with well-defined accountability", replacing "the original requirement for annual board approval of model risk management policies and specific board reporting requirements".
note: Important counter-signal. US regulators REMOVED the board approval requirement and carved generative and agentic AI out of model risk scope entirely. This weakens the 'regulation will force US bank boards to get trained on AI models' thesis, and leaves genAI governed by nothing specific. Contradicts REG013 (India tightening). Record both.

skill: DORA management body ICT knowledge obligation
metric: "Members of the management body of the financial entity shall actively keep up to date with sufficient knowledge and skills to understand and assess ICT risk".
note: One of very few regulations anywhere that places a personal continuing-education duty directly on board members. Already in force (DORA applied from Jan 2025). This is genuine board-programme demand in EU financial services, and the cleanest legal citation available for selling a director-level tech-risk module. Page pub date not stated; the Regulation is 2022/2554.

skill: RBI operational resilience - segmented training by seniority
source: PwC India on RBI Guidance Note
metric: Issued 30 April 2024. Applies to commercial banks, urban/state/central co-operative banks, all-India financial institutions and all NBFCs including HFCs. Requires "Board to set the tone at the top with strong culture of risk management and ethical business practices"; "Segmented operational risk training based on the seniority, role and responsibilities"; "Board is responsible and accountable for oversight over ORMF and also for performing regular review".
note: Explicitly mandates training segmented BY SENIORITY across the entire Indian banking and NBFC system. That is close to a written specification for a tiered executive programme. No hard deadline attached, which is why it has not produced a visible procurement spike - but it is standing regulatory cover for anyone in an Indian bank who wants to buy a board/senior risk programme.

skill: SEBI CSCRF tiered cyber resilience obligations
metric: Framework applies to "22 types of SEBI-regulated entities" across five tiers (MII, Qualified RE, Mid-size RE, Small-size RE, Self-cert RE). Master framework effective 20 August 2024; April 2025 amendments reclassified brokers; August 2025 clarifications softened ISO 27001 from mandatory to "recommended". "IT Committee [is] Quarterly + cyber expert" for MII through Mid-size tiers.
note: Requirement for a cyber expert on the IT committee is a board-composition signal, not a training mandate. Mostly CISO/compliance demand. Classify as specialist demand, with a narrow director-level cyber literacy add-on for market infrastructure institutions.

skill: IICA independent director databank registration and proficiency test
metric: "Every Individual - Who has been appointed as an Independent Director in a company...and is going to be appointed" must register. Non-exempt individuals must "pass an online proficiency self-assessment test conducted by the institute within a period of two years from the date of inclusion of his name in the databank". Pass mark: "a score of not less than fifty percent in aggregate". Legal basis: Rule 6(4), Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Fifth Amendment Rules, 2019.
note: A standing, non-discretionary certification obligation on every Indian independent director, with broad exemptions (3+ years as director/KMP, 10 years as CA/CS/advocate). Because the exemptions cover most experienced directors and the pass mark is 50%, it generates low-value test-prep demand, NOT premium executive education. Negative finding for anyone hoping to sell an ISB board programme on the back of it - the compliance need is already met cheaply. The opportunity is adjacent (AI/climate/cyber board literacy, which the databank does not cover).

skill: India GCC growth and leadership capability gap
metric: Headline: "India's GCC Boom Enters Its Next Test: Talent, Skills And Leadership".
note: Could not open - 403. Headline alone supports the direction (GCC leadership capability named as the binding constraint) but no figure is verifiable from it. Flagged for a second pass with a different source (NASSCOM/EY GCC reports). T13.S02.P03 remains the best-fitting topic and is marked [New] in the taxonomy, consistent with this being an emerging need.

skill: India clean energy jobs to 2030
metric: "44 lakh (4.4 million) full-time equivalent jobs" by 2030 across India's clean energy sector; "nearly 60% of deployment-related jobs require highly skilled or semi-skilled workers"; "80-90% in manufacturing"; "around 13 lakh FTE jobs will be concentrated in operations, maintenance, and manufacturing roles".
note: NEGATIVE FINDING for executive education. The CEEW-NRDC data quantifies technician and installer demand, not managerial demand - the report provides no breakdown of managerial, supervisory or business-development roles. India's energy transition is a large vocational-skilling market and only a small executive market. Do not use the 44 lakh figure as evidence for a senior energy-transition programme; it is evidence for the opposite.

skill: India defence indigenisation targets and private-sector share
source: Press Information Bureau, Government of India
metric: "India recorded its highest-ever defence production of Rs 1.54 lakh crore in FY 2024-25"; exports "Rs 23,622 crore in FY 2024-25", up "12.04%". Targets: "defence manufacturing worth Rs. 3 lakh crore" and "Rs 50,000 crore in defence exports by 2029". Private sector contribution "23%" of production. "788 industrial licenses have been issued to 462 companies"; "16,000 MSMEs".
note: The 2029 target implies roughly doubling production inside the study window, from a base where private industry is only 23%. 462 licensed companies and 16,000 MSMEs scaling into defence is a real general-management and offsets/compliance capability gap. But there is no obligation to train anyone - this is sector-shift demand, discretionary, and the addressable population is small. Better as a niche programme than a theme.

skill: ABDM compliance mandate for AB-PMJAY empanelled hospitals
metric: Private hospitals empanelled under AB-PMJAY must "Adopt ABDM-certified HMIS / HIS solutions", "Submit all insurance claims directly through the PMJAY Transaction Management" and "Integrate claim data via the ABDM network". Cited rationale includes "fake or duplicate patient admissions" and "inflated or invalid insurance claims".
note: Binds hospital operators, but the capability required is systems integration and claims process redesign - a hospital-IT and revenue-cycle problem. Creates specialist demand, not executive-education demand, with the exception of hospital CEO/owner briefings on digital-health operating models (T12.S01.P04). No exact deadline date could be verified from this source.

skill: India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 and semiconductor talent requirement
metric: Headline: "Semiconductor talent: The foundation of India's next technology revolution".
note: Could not open - 403. India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 was announced in Budget 2026 (per PIB Feb 2026 document seen in search results) but no figure verified. Semiconductor/PLI demand is almost entirely engineering-level; the executive slice is plant leadership and manufacturing strategy (T06.S01.P04), which is a small cohort. Treat as unverified and low priority.

skill: Board and C-suite AI literacy as a named regulatory expectation (missing topic)
source: Synthesis of REG001, REG004, REG012, REG015
metric: No single source; concept recurs verbatim across EU AI Act Art 4, DORA Art 5(4) and RBI FREE-AI ("capacity building ... particularly at the board and C-suite levels, to ensure AI literacy and readiness").
note: TAXONOMY GAP. The list has T03.S01.P04 'Data and AI literacy for non-technical leaders' and T03.S02.P05 'Board oversight of AI' as separate topics, but nothing for the regulator-driven, evidence-producing version: a board/ExCo AI-literacy programme that a company can point to as its Article 4 / DORA / FREE-AI compliance artefact. That certification-with-evidence framing is what makes the sale non-discretionary and is the highest-conviction new product in this research.

skill: GCC scale: 2,117 GCCs, 2.36Mn talent, $98.4Bn FY2026; 'Centers built for delivery are increasingly holding global ownership'
metric: "2,117 GCCs in India" across "3,728 GCC units" employing "2.36Mn talent"; "$98.4Bn market" FY2026; "32% growth since FY2021"; "506 Forbes Global 2000 companies operate a GCC in India". "The strategic role of India GCCs has fundamentally changed. Most enterprise operating models have not."
note: The authoritative India-specific structural signal. Scale alone is not a leadership-education signal; the operating-model sentence is. T13.S02.P03 is the only topic that names GCCs and it is flagged [New] - correctly.

skill: Global roles held from India GCCs: 115 (2015) to 6,500+ (2024), projected 30,000 by 2030
source: Zinnov, 'The Rise of Global Roles in India'
metric: Pari Natarajan, CEO Zinnov: "The number of global roles in India GCCs has grown from a mere 115 in 2015 and is projected to grow to 30,000 by 2030." Indian GCC leaders now responsible for "driving financial performance, making core technology decisions, and influencing enterprise architecture and processes."
note: ~23,500 net new global P&L/enterprise-scope roles to be filled from India between now and 2030. This is the single best-quantified India-specific senior-leader demand pool in this whole scan. Maps to T01.S02.P03 (leading the enterprise), T01.S02.P05 (leading a P&L), T14.S01.P06 (cross-cultural) and T13.S02.P03.

skill: GCC leadership AI literacy at 27%; 90%+ of GCCs say 40% or fewer of their leaders have enough AI literacy for strategic decisions
source: PwC-FICCI GCC survey (200 senior GCC executives)
metric: "Leadership AI literacy at only 27% on average"; "Over 90% report 40% or fewer leaders have sufficient AI literacy for strategic decisions"; "72% of GCCs need to reskill/upskill over 40% of their workforce"; "94% believe talent development spending must rise to at least 6% of operating budgets (from current 3-5%)"; "86% expect AI to bring substantial or transformational change by 2030"
note: Strongest single India signal for AI-fluency-for-leaders. Note it is a stated-intent survey, not behaviour. The 3-5% to 6% budget line is a direct addressable-spend signal for exec ed. Supports T01.S04.P03, T03.S01.P04, T03.S01.P01, T13.S02.P03.

skill: 62% of GCCs cite lack of professionals combining domain expertise with tech skills; 'composite skills that combine AI capabilities with domain knowledge'
metric: "62% cite lack of professionals combining domain expertise with tech skills"; Rajesh Ojha, PwC India: "composite skills that combine AI capabilities with domain knowledge"; "57% want AI/digital modules in engineering and management curricula"
note: The gap named is a hybrid, not a pure-AI, gap. Argues against standalone AI courses and for AI-plus-function formats. Supports T03.S01.P04, T15.S01.P02.

skill: GCC senior leadership pipeline not being built internally; missing capabilities named as global stakeholder management, strategic influence with HQ, AI and data governance, crisis and risk management
metric: "Senior leadership roles in GCCs are disproportionately filled through external hiring rather than internal promotion, which signals that the pipeline is not being built." Gaps named: "Global stakeholder management; Strategic influence with headquarters; AI and data governance; Crisis and risk management; Internal talent development". "58% of GCCs take 45+ days to fill critical roles".
note: Trade-press analysis, weaker than NASSCOM/PwC, but the capability list is unusually precise and none of it is technical. 'Strategic influence with headquarters' has no home in the 223-topic list - closest are T14.S02.P04 and T07.S04.P05, both of which miss the cross-border-principal-agent character. Possible missing topic.

skill: AI may reduce entry-level absorption in GCCs while managerial orchestration demand grows; 40k-150k displacement by 2030
source: ORF, 'Capability in the Age of AI: India's GCCs and the Future of White-Collar Work'
metric: "AI may reduce entry-level absorption even if aggregate GCC output continues" expanding; conservative scenario "~40,000 jobs displaced by 2030", aggressive "~150,000 jobs displaced by 2030" against a 4-4.5Mn 2030 baseline; "enterprise transformation requires human orchestration, domain judgement, and organisational capability"; new roles in "AI governance and model supervision, data quality management, compliance automation oversight, human-machine workflow design".
note: Important corrective: the projected GCC displacement is small (1-3% of the 2030 base) and concentrated at entry level. The managerial layer is described as the thing AI needs more of, not less. Supports T01.S04.P02, T01.S04.P01, T03.S02.P01.

skill: RBI FREE-AI framework mandates board-level accountability for AI in all regulated financial entities
source: RBI FREE-AI Committee Report (via Humaine Eti summary)
metric: Pillar 4 Governance: "Board-level accountability, reporting, and oversight of AI initiatives. AI disclosures move from optional to part of the annual report." Board-approved AI policies covering "AI lifecycle management, risk controls, and third-party vendor liabilities" with board sign-off and annual reviews; a designated executive (Chief AI Officer or equivalent) holding "accountability for AI risk, with quarterly board reporting". Pillar 3 Capacity: "Building AI skills, knowledge sharing, and expertise in fairness and explainability across the sector."
note: Non-discretionary. Every Indian bank, NBFC, insurer board now needs AI-governance literacy, and a named Chief AI Officer role is being created wholesale. Strongest India regulatory driver for T03.S02.P05, T08.S01.P04, T03.S02.P01, T13.S01.P01. Note: summary is secondary; primary PDF is rbidocs.rbi.org.in.

skill: DPDP Act substantive obligations and penalties commence 13 May 2027; Rules notified 13 Nov 2025
metric: "The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified on 13 November 2025"; "On 13 May 2027 the substantive obligations of the Act commence: notice under Section 5, consent under Section 6, general obligations and security safeguards under Section 8", with penalty provisions taking effect simultaneously; maximum penalty "INR 250 crore" for failure of reasonable security safeguards; Significant Data Fiduciaries face "Mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessments and independent audits", DPO appointment and 72-hour breach notification.
note: A hard-dated compliance cliff inside the study window. Demand for DPDP-literate managers peaks FY2026-27, i.e. exactly 2027. Supports T03.S05.P02, T03.S02.P03, T08.S02.P03. Secondary source - verify date against MeitY/PIB primary.

skill: BRSR Core value-chain reporting for top 250 listed entities from FY2024-25; assurance/assessment glide path for top 1,000
source: Uniqus, BRSR reporting and assurance framework update
metric: "top 250 listed entities" must report BRSR Core for their value chain "from Financial Year (FY) 2024-25 onwards"; "top 1,000 listed entities" subject to phased assurance; SEBI "substituted the term 'assurance' with 'assurance or assessment'"; value chain partners "cumulatively comprising 75% of their purchases/sales (by value)".
note: Value-chain scope is the demand multiplier: the obligation propagates from 250 listed firms to thousands of unlisted suppliers whose managers must produce auditable ESG data. India's BRSR is a stronger near-term driver than CSRD is for Indian firms. Supports T10.S02.P01, T10.S01.P01, T06.S02.P02.

skill: Statutory director proficiency test: every individual in the IICA Independent Directors Databank must pass within two years of registration
source: IICA / Companies Act s.150(1) (via iPleaders guide)
metric: "Every individual whose name appears in the Independent Directors Databank maintained by the Indian Institute of Corporate Affairs must pass the Online Proficiency Self-Assessment Test within two years of registration." Syllabus: Companies Law, Securities Law, Basic Accountancy, Corporate Governance. "An individual who has obtained a score of not less than 50% in aggregate shall be deemed to have passed such test." Basis: Section 150(1) Companies Act 2013 and Rule 6(4).
note: India has a statutory, examined board-readiness requirement that the US and EU do not. It creates guaranteed volume for T08.S01.P01/P02 but caps price - the test itself is cheap and self-assessed. The exec-ed opportunity is the gap the syllabus does NOT cover: AI, cyber, ESG oversight (T08.S01.P04, T10.S02.P02, T03.S05.P01).

skill: NITI Aayog Roadmap for Job Creation in the AI Economy: up to 4 million new jobs in five years across a 9-million-professional, $245bn sector
source: NITI Aayog / PIB (with NASSCOM and BCG)
metric: "Up to 4 million new jobs" can be created in the next five years across "9 million technology and customer experience professionals" in a "$245 billion" sector; three pillars: embed AI literacy across education, "build national reskilling engine for tech/CX professionals", position India as a global AI talent magnet; at-risk roles named as QA engineers and L1 support agents; emerging roles include Ethical AI Specialists and AI Trainers.
note: Government framing is overwhelmingly about technical and entry-level roles. NITI Aayog does NOT name a managerial or leadership capability gap. That absence is itself a finding: India's official AI-skilling narrative has no leadership layer, which is where an exec-ed provider has unclaimed ground.

skill: India's Management Capability Development Index fell from ~76 (2011) to 69.7 (2024); 'Innovation and Adaptability' the worst-performing dimension
source: KPMG India / AIMA Management Capability Development Index India 2024
metric: MCDI score declined "from around 76 to 69.7 in 2024, reflecting stagnant growth in management capabilities", ~8.3% since 2011; "Innovation and Adaptability" the worst-performing dimension in 2024, down ~10% since 2011; "Integrity and Corporate Governance" highest-ranked throughout; "core capabilities like organisation capability and application of technology and knowledge show only modest improvements". Sample: 200 senior leaders including CEOs and CXOs.
note: Rare longitudinal India-specific measure of managerial quality, and it is going backwards over 13 years. Directly supports foundational and general-management topics (T01.S01.*, T15.S01.P01) against the assumption that classic management content is saturated. Also supports T09.S01.P01 via the innovation-capability decline.

skill: AI/ML hiring +31% YoY, GCC hiring +10% YoY; hiring for 16+ years experience more than doubled and 13-16 years +87%
metric: "AI/ML Hiring: 31% year-on-year increase"; "GCC hiring: 10% growth"; white-collar hiring +14% YoY, index "rose to 3,028 points from 2,664"; experience bands: "16+ years experience: More than doubled", "13-16 years experience: 87% increase", "8-12 years experience: 39% rise". GCC growth by city: Hyderabad 28%, Chennai 21%, Pune 15%, Bengaluru 13%.
note: Behavioural, not stated intent - the strongest evidence class in this scan. Senior-band postings are growing several times faster than the overall market, which is the opposite of the global 'AI flattens middle management' narrative. Directly supports T01.S02.*, T13.S02.P03 and undercuts the assumption that senior demand is soft.

skill: India executive education and upskilling market USD 12.2bn (2025) to USD 27.3bn (2032), 12.21% CAGR; digital and technology upskilling is the dominant revenue pool
source: Ken Research, India Executive Education and Upskilling Market
metric: "2025 Market Value: USD 12,200 million; 2032 Projection: USD 27,320 million; CAGR (2025-2032): 12.21%"; segments: "Digital and Technology Upskilling (dominant revenue pool), Executive Leadership Education, Functional and Professional Upskilling, Managed Enterprise Learning"; "Blended Hybrid programs are positioned for the strongest premiumization because they preserve flexibility while supporting peer networking"; "90% of surveyed Indian professionals (2025, India) consider AI and GenAI expertise critical for future-proofing careers".
note: Treat the absolute numbers as contested - Ken Research separately publishes an India executive education market of INR 1,480 crore (~USD 175mn), roughly 70x smaller, because it scopes the category differently. Use the CAGR and the segment ordering, not the level. The blended-hybrid premiumisation finding is the actionable part.

skill: Contradictory Indian market sizing: same research house reports INR 1,480 Cr executive education and USD 12.91bn corporate training
metric: Headline: "Ken Research Stated India Executive Education Market Reached INR 1,480 Cr"; separate headline: "Ken Research Stated India Corporate Training Market to Reach USD 12.91 Billion".
note: Could not open either page (403). Recorded because the contradiction is the finding: Indian exec-ed market sizes in circulation differ by up to two orders of magnitude depending on whether corporate L&D spend is included. Any business case built on a single Indian market-size number is unsafe.

skill: 85% of Indian employers report some AI or GenAI use but only 13% have adoption across more than half their workforce
source: TeamLease Employment Outlook Report H2 FY27 (via Business Standard)
metric: "85 per cent of employers report some level of AI or GenAI use, only 13 per cent have adoption across more than half of their workforce." Net employment change projected at 5.4% for H2 FY27, "the highest level in the past four half-year periods"; "72 per cent expect moderate to significant difficulty in hiring".
note: The 85/13 split is the adoption-depth gap. It means the binding constraint in India is diffusion through the organisation - a management problem - not tool access. Best evidence for T01.S04.P03 and T03.S03.P01 as distinct from T03.S01.P02.

skill: 'Commercial acumen is becoming increasingly important for senior leadership appointments in engineering and manufacturing'
source: Michael Page India Salary Guide 2026 and TeamLease (via Business Today)
metric: Average increments "8-12% in 2026"; premium skills hikes "up to 30% when changing jobs", and at Rs 50 lakh-plus "hikes of 40-45%". "Commercial acumen is becoming increasingly important for senior leadership appointments in engineering and manufacturing." Premium skills listed: AI/ML, semiconductors, renewable energy, automotive, battery technologies, cloud management, cybersecurity, data.
note: Pay data is behaviour-adjacent. The 40-45% premium at the Rs 50 lakh-plus band says the scarcity is at senior level. The commercial-acumen line supports finance-for-non-finance and P&L topics (T04.S01.P01, T04.S01.P05, T01.S02.P05) for technical seniors - a classic India exec-ed segment.

skill: NASSCOM AI Adoption Index 2.0 names 'leadership commitment to AI being inconsistent' as a top barrier across 500 Indian companies
metric: Adoption score "2.47 on a 4-point scale (compared to 2.45 in 2022)"; "87% of companies are in the middle stages of Enthusiast and Expert AI adopters"; "2X rise in the number of companies at the Expert stage in 2024 versus 2022". Barriers: "Leadership commitment to AI being inconsistent" reflected in ad-hoc proof-of-concept strategies; use case selection difficulties; AI-led innovation "very nascent and lagging". 500 companies across seven sectors representing 75% of India's GDP.
note: India's own tech industry body puts leadership, not technology or engineering talent, first on the barrier list. The score barely moved 2022-2024 (2.45 to 2.47) despite the GenAI wave - adoption is stalling at the management layer. Supports T01.S04.P03, T03.S01.P05, T02.S03.P01.

skill: NASSCOM chief: India Inc has 5-10 years of AI implementation runway even if innovation stopped today; barrier is 'enterprise friction'
metric: "Once, let's say all AI stopped today... we still have five to ten years to implement the best AI right now, if we even stop progress." Main obstacle is "enterprise friction": budget constraints, data readiness, talent shortages, legal considerations, accuracy and reputational risk. "For the first time, we have an opportunity to not face that problem, because today, AI is coming as an opex, rather than capex for most organisations."
note: Reframes the 2027-2031 India demand: the scarce capability is implementation and change management, not frontier-model knowledge. Argues for T01.S05.P01, T03.S03.P01, T03.S01.P05 over T03.S01.P02. The opex-not-capex point is a genuine India-specific mechanism - it removes the capital barrier that historically slowed Indian IT adoption.

skill: India produces ~2,500 hospital management professionals a year against a current requirement of 21,000+ and ~45,000 needed by 2030
source: Study reported by Outlook India Healthcare Spotlight
metric: "India currently produces approximately 2,500 hospital management professionals annually" against a "current requirement: over 21,000 professionals" and a "projected requirement by 2030: around 45,000 health management professionals". Only "74 postgraduate seats in hospital administration recognized by the National Medical Commission", about "0.15% of all postgraduate medical seats". Survey of 574 healthcare professionals and students: "46% of medical students reported little or no information about hospital administration".
note: An order-of-magnitude supply shortfall in a topic the taxonomy already carries (T12.S01.P01) and a natural exec-ed rather than degree market, because the demand is clinicians already in post. Also supports T12.S02.P03 (clinical leadership for doctors). India-specific: the bottleneck is regulated PG seats, which exec ed sidesteps entirely.

skill: CONTRADICTION: foundit Insights Tracker reports Senior Management function hiring -13% YoY and 15+ years experience -11%, against Naukri's 16+ years more than doubling
metric: Overall index "-10%" YoY, "+5%" MoM, "-18%" over 6 months. By experience: "7-10 years: +10%" the only segment with annual growth; "11-15 years: -2%"; "15+ years: -11%"; "0-3 years: -9%". By function, Senior Management "-13%". "firms are pulling back on volume hiring at the junior end and on leadership expansion at the top, while retaining appetite for the mid-career layer."
note: Directly contradicts row IN013 (Naukri JobSpeak, same month, same market). Both are job-posting counts. Likely explanation: different employer mixes and index bases - Naukri skews IT/GCC white-collar, foundit broader. Net reading: senior demand is concentrated in GCC and AI-adjacent employers and weak elsewhere, which sharpens rather than weakens the GCC-leadership thesis. Do not cite either number alone.

skill: India Skills Report 2026: employability 56.35%; persistent employer concerns on communication, problem-solving, teamwork and critical thinking despite technical competence
source: India Skills Report 2026 (ETS, CII, AICTE, AIU, Taggd) via InsightsonIndia
metric: Overall employability "56.35% (from ~54.8%)", "almost a 10-percentage point jump in about 4 years". "AI, data analytics, automation, cloud, cybersecurity dominate roles". "persistent concerns around communication skills, problem-solving, teamwork and critical thinking" despite technical competence. Companies plan to hire "40% more people" next year (up from 29%). "Gig hiring grew ~38%" with gigs "around 16% of all jobs".
note: Weak evidence for this study - the ISR measures entry-level employability, not managerial capability. Recorded for completeness and because the named gaps are communication and critical thinking, not AI. Supports T14.S01.P04, T14.S02.P02, T14.S01.P03 as durable India demand that AI does not displace.

skill: NITI Aayog MSME green transition roadmap: a dedicated national institute for energy and greening plus cluster capacity building, over a 10-year implementation
source: NITI Aayog, Roadmap for Green Transition of MSMEs
metric: "a dedicated 'MSME National-Level Institute for Energy and Greening' will be required to be established under the aegis of the Ministry of MSME"; the NPMA "to also lead the demand aggregation efforts to maximise the uptake of green transition efforts in selected MSME clusters. This will involve capacity building on the three identified levers/solutions"; "MSMEs are unaware of the technologies and performance guarantee models run by energy services companies".
note: Government is explicitly funding owner-manager capability building for decarbonisation. Pairs with the BRSR value-chain obligation (IN009): listed firms push ESG data requirements down to MSME suppliers while NITI Aayog funds the MSMEs' capacity. Supports T10.S01.P02, T10.S01.P03, T09.S02.P05, T15.S01.P04.

skill: GCC India headcount projected to reach 4-4.5 million by 2030 from ~2.3 million, implying a managerial layer several times its current size
source: ORF, 'Capability in the Age of AI: India's GCCs'
metric: "Current (FY2024): 1,700+ GCCs generating $64.6 billion annually, employing ~1.9 million professionals"; "Projected (FY2026): 2,100+ centers with 2.3 million employees and ~$100 billion revenue"; "2030 Target: 4-4.5 million employees across the sector".
note: At any plausible span of control, doubling GCC headcount by 2030 requires roughly 100,000-200,000 additional people managers and several thousand additional senior leaders in India in the study window. No Indian business school currently runs a GCC-leadership programme at that scale. This is the clearest unmet-supply argument in the scan.

skill: Agent boss / managing AI agents as a team
metric: 'Agent Boss': a professional who builds, delegates to and manages AI agents to expand impact and scale faster. 81% of leaders expect moderate-to-extensive agent integration into their AI strategy within 12-18 months. 28% of leaders are considering hiring AI workforce managers. Survey of 31,000 knowledge workers across 31 countries.
note: Vendor-sponsored and definitionally self-serving, but it is the framing that has travelled furthest into leadership vocabulary. 'Human-agent ratio' and 'work chart' (outcome-based teams replacing function-based org charts) are the two concepts ISB could own as a course.

skill: Redesigning managerial work around AI / work chart replacing org chart
metric: 'Work Chart': dynamic, outcome-driven organisational model replacing traditional function-based org charts, with teams forming around goals powered by AI agents. 82% of leaders say 2025 is a pivotal year to rethink strategy and operations. 51% of managers say AI training will be a core responsibility within five years.
note: 51% of managers expecting AI training to become a core managerial responsibility is the single most course-relevant number here: it makes capability-building a line-manager job, not an L&D job.

skill: Building AI fluency and adoption in the workforce; manager modelling effect
metric: When managers actively model AI use there is a 17-point lift in reported AI value, a 22-point lift in critical thinking about AI, and a 30-point lift in trust in agentic AI. Where managers create psychological safety, employees are 1.4x more likely to be high-frequency agentic AI users. Organisational factors account for more than 2x the reported AI impact of individual factors (67% vs 32%). 20,000 knowledge workers, 10 countries, Feb-Apr 2026.
note: This is the strongest available argument that AI adoption is a *management* problem, not a tools problem — i.e. it belongs in leadership programmes, not technical ones. Note the organisational-vs-individual 67/32 split: it directly undercuts the 'train individuals in prompting' model of exec ed.

skill: Trust, accountability and human oversight of AI decisions
source: Harvard Business Review — Kropp Bedard Wiles Hsu Krayer (BCG)
metric: Large-scale experiment found anthropomorphising AI agents reduced individual accountability among human workers, increased unnecessary escalation of decisions, lowered quality of work reviews, increased confusion about role definitions, and produced no improvement in AI adoption. Leaders should focus on 'redesigning workflows, roles, and governance so humans remain clearly accountable while effectively supervising increasingly capable systems.'
note: Rare HBR piece with an actual experiment behind it, so grade it above normal HBR opinion. Useful because it argues AGAINST the Microsoft 'agent boss' framing — teach accountability design, not agent-as-teammate.

skill: Managers' share of time spent directing AI rather than doing work
metric: 47% of workers spend more time managing and directing AI than doing the work themselves. 72% report AI has considerably changed skill requirements. 30% have agents integrated into workflows, doubled from 13% a year earlier. 11,749 workers across 14 markets.
note: 'Managing AI' becoming the majority of the job for nearly half the workforce is a behaviour-adjacent measure, stronger than intent. Supervision/delegation/quality-assurance is now a mass skill, not an elite one.

skill: Managers and leaders expect agents to absorb half their own role
metric: 65% of managers and leaders expect AI agents to handle at least 50% of their role within three years. 61% of all respondents believe agents could handle at least half their job within three years. 52% have limited understanding of agent capabilities.
note: Self-reported expectation, so intent not behaviour — but the seniority cut is exactly the study's period and audience. The 65%-expect vs 52%-don't-understand gap is a straightforward programme hook.

skill: Frontline AI adoption highest in India
metric: India, the Middle East, Brazil and South Africa lead adoption among frontline workers, exceeding the global average and most developed nations; the US, France and Italy lag. 74% of frontline employees are regular AI users, up 23 percentage points year-over-year. 66% receive limited or no guidance on redirecting saved time; over 50% don't redirect time into strategic work.
note: India-specific and important for ISB positioning: the Indian constraint is not tool adoption, it is managerial redesign of what to do with freed capacity. That is a general-management problem.

skill: Middle managers as the bottleneck in AI adoption — workload not headcount
source: Harvard Business Review — Julia Shin and Sandra J. Sucher
metric: 18 semi-structured interviews at two major consulting firms. Senior leaders expand scope and junior consultants gain productivity, but middle managers absorb three new burdens — validating AI-generated outputs, identifying and correcting errors, and coaching teams on AI skills — under 'unchanged or even increased delivery pressure' and without formal support structures. The middle layer is 'a critical bottleneck'.
note: Directly relevant to the middle-management question and points the OPPOSITE way to the flattening story: the role is being loaded, not deleted. Small qualitative sample (n=18, two firms) so grade the generalisation cautiously. No taxonomy topic covers 'supervising and quality-assuring AI output as a managerial discipline' — closest is T01.S04.P04 but that is framed as governance, not as day-to-day workload.

skill: Middle managers determine whether AI adoption succeeds
metric: 'The most common failure point in generative AI is not the boardroom, the vendor shortlist, or the training portal. It is the layer of managers who must turn executive ambition into everyday behavior.' Identifies five manager profiles: AI skeptics, wait-and-see traditionalists, cautious implementers, enthusiastic experimenters, AI catalysts.
note: Expert opinion, no data — grade low on evidence, high on audience salience. Consistent with WH03 (Microsoft's manager-modelling lift), which gives the assertion empirical backing from another source.

skill: AI is squeezing middle managers
source: Harvard Business Review — Gretchen Gavett (The Insider)
metric: Headline and standfirst: 'AI Is Squeezing Middle Managers' — describing 'new research showing how AI adoption is overloading middle managers.'
note: Could not open the body (newsletter page returned metadata only). Recorded because HBR chose to run the squeeze framing as a headline twice in one month — that is a signal about what the leadership audience is being told, even if the underlying research is WH08.

skill: Span of control roughly doubled in five years
metric: 'There are now nearly six individual contributors per manager at the 8,500 small businesses analyzed' (September 2024), up 'from a little over three in 2019'. Chart: 3.15 (Jan 2019) to 5.76 (Sep 2024). 'People managers now oversee about twice as many workers as just five years ago.' Google 'cut vice president and manager roles by 10% last year'. Gusto economist Nich Tremper: 'It's happening broadly across the economy' — mostly via attrition, where 'an existing one will just see an expanded scope.'
note: The hardest behavioural evidence I found on the flattening side — payroll data, not a survey. Two caveats for ISB: it is US small business (8,500 firms on Gusto), and the mechanism is attrition with expanded scope, i.e. FEWER managers each doing a BIGGER job. That is a demand-reducing signal for volume and a demand-increasing signal for capability per manager. Gusto's own research also reportedly found 'industries with more managers had higher worker productivity.'

skill: Headcount change by seniority level under AI — India
source: PwC 29th Annual Global CEO Survey: India perspective
metric: 54% of India CEOs expect junior-level employment to decrease within three years due to AI adoption (vs 49% globally); 30% expect mid-level positions to remain stable; 19% anticipate senior-level increases. 66% of India CEOs are concerned about keeping pace with technology/AI (vs 42% globally). 41% believe current AI investments are insufficient to meet company goals. 43% successfully attract high-quality AI talent. 36% report unnecessary bureaucratic processes inhibiting performance.
note: This is the most direct answer to the middle-management question I found. CEOs expect the squeeze at the JUNIOR level, not the middle: mid-level stable, senior rising. It contradicts the flattening narrative for India specifically. Caveat: stated intent, and 'stable' was offered as an option so it may be the low-effort answer.

skill: CEO agenda 2026 — AI has not yet paid
metric: 4,454 CEOs across 95 countries, surveyed 30 Sep - 10 Nov 2025. 'Only 12% of CEOs report AI has delivered both cost and revenue benefits'; 33% report gains in either; 56% have seen no significant financial benefit to date. Only 30% of CEOs are confident about revenue growth in the next 12 months, down from 38% in 2025. More than 42% of companies have begun competing in new sectors over the past five years.
note: Important corrective to the AI-skills-are-everything thesis: the majority of CEOs report NO financial benefit from AI so far. If ROI stays absent through 2027, demand tilts back toward classic value-creation content (strategy, capital allocation, execution) rather than more AI courses. The 42% competing in new sectors is a strategy/M&A demand signal (T02.S01.P02, T02.S05.P01).

skill: Reinvention and competing in new sectors — India
source: PwC 29th Annual Global CEO Survey: India perspective
metric: 57% of India CEOs report their companies have competed in new sectors over the last five years, up from 39% in 2025. 50% acknowledge innovation as vital to business strategy; 48% lack high risk tolerance for innovation projects; 43% don't collaborate with external partners on innovation (vs 31% globally).
note: An 18-point jump in one year on cross-sector competition is a strong demand signal for business-model reinvention and corporate strategy — and it is a general-management argument, not an AI one.

skill: Adaptability and change capacity as the binding constraint
metric: 85% of leaders say adaptability is critical but only 7% say they are successfully helping their workforce adapt. Only 27% of leaders say their organisations manage change well. One-third of workers experienced 15 or more major changes annually. 7 in 10 business leaders prioritise speed and agility.
note: 85%-vs-7% is the widest say-do gap in this whole dataset and it is about change leadership, a classic non-AI capability. Strong evidence for T01.S05.P01 and T07.S04.P01.

skill: AI governance gap — executives use AI in decisions but cannot govern it
metric: 60% of executives use AI in decisions; only 5% say they manage AI well. 65% believe culture needs significant change because of AI; 34% say culture inhibits AI transformation goals. Only 6% are making progress on designing human-AI interaction. 56% design AI for business outcomes only, 40% for both business and human outcomes. 42% of workers say their organisations don't evaluate AI's impact on people.
note: The 60/5 split is the cleanest AI-governance demand number available. Note it is governance of DECISIONS, which is closer to T03.S04.P06 (AI-augmented decision-making and judgment) than to regulatory compliance — the taxonomy splits these and the market may not.

skill: Org design shifting from structure to flow; flattening delivering diminishing returns
metric: 10,018 senior executives across 15 countries and 16 industries (survey Jun-Sep 2025). 'Two-thirds of leaders think their organizations are overly complex and inefficient, but traditional remedies relying on structural redesigns, cost cuts, and flatter hierarchies are achieving diminishing returns.' Where AI eliminated positions, '54 percent of leaders upskilled, reskilled, or redeployed the affected employees, and only one in ten eliminated the role entirely.' AI 'puts even greater emphasis on the human aspects of work and requires more of leaders.'
note: This is McKinsey explicitly saying flattening is hitting diminishing returns — a direct contradiction of the Great Flattening narrative, from a 10,000-executive base. Combined with 'only one in ten eliminated the role entirely', it is the strongest evidence that managerial demand is being redefined rather than destroyed.

skill: Reflective leadership capacity correlates with organisational adaptability
metric: '30% of reflective leaders believe their organizations can quickly adapt to change, versus only 17 percent of non-reflective leaders.'
note: Correlational and self-reported, so weak as causal evidence. Recorded because it is a large-n consultancy making a classic, non-AI leadership-development argument (reflection, self-awareness) in an AI report — supports T14.S02.P05.

skill: Agentic AI scaling concentrated in large enterprises
source: McKinsey The State of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI
metric: 1,719 participants across 97 nations. '40 percent of respondents from large organizations (>$1B revenue) report scaling AI agents', up from 27%, versus 22% at smaller organisations (flat). High performers (6% of respondents) 'fundamentally redesign workflows rather than layer AI onto existing ones' and are '3.3 times more likely than others to intend to use AI to fundamentally transform their business.' 'The limiting factor is increasingly the organization's ability to absorb change.'
note: 'Ability to absorb change' being named the limiting factor is the same finding as Deloitte's 85/7 gap from an independent source. Two large-n consultancies converging on change capacity, not AI skill, as the binding constraint.

skill: AI strain falls disproportionately on middle managers
source: McKinsey The State of AI in 2026
metric: Negative effects by role: executives and senior managers 31% report AI-related strain; midlevel managers and individual contributors 47%.
note: A 16-point seniority gap in reported strain. Corroborates the HBR Shin/Sucher bottleneck finding (WH08) with a much larger sample. Argues for middle-manager-specific programming rather than generic leadership content.

skill: Leadership alignment and psychological safety as AI prerequisites
metric: Only 26% of AI users say their leadership is 'clearly and consistently aligned on AI'. 81% of leaders report feeling safe suggesting new AI work approaches vs 67% of employees. 65% of AI users fear falling behind without AI adaptation, but 45% say it feels safer to focus on current goals than redesign work, and only 13% report being rewarded for work reinvention if results don't materialise.
note: The 65-fear / 45-play-safe / 13-rewarded chain is a classic incentive-design and psychological-safety problem dressed as an AI problem. Supports T01.S03.P05 and T07.S02.P02 (performance management) more than it supports any AI topic.

skill: Core skill ranking — leadership and social influence rising fastest in importance
metric: 'Leadership and social influence, resilience, flexibility and agility, and AI and big data have seen the most substantial increase in importance, with 22, 17, and 17 percentage-point rises, respectively' (since 2023). Core skills 2025 top five: analytical thinking (seven out of 10 companies consider it essential), resilience/flexibility/agility, leadership and social influence, creative thinking, motivation and self-awareness. Employers expect 39% of workers' core skills to change by 2030, down from 44% in 2023.
note: This is the single best evidenced answer to the second question. Leadership and social influence rose MORE than AI and big data (22pp vs 17pp) between the 2023 and 2025 waves, from the same employer sample. Also note the disruption estimate FELL from 44% to 39% — employers are becoming less apocalyptic, not more.

skill: CPO priorities — job redesign ahead of reskilling
source: WEF Chief People Officers' Outlook May 2026
metric: 140+ chief people officers from large global employers, surveyed 15 Jan - 2 Mar 2026. 74% prioritise reviewing organisational structure and job design; 70% prioritise expanding upskilling and reskilling programmes. 'AI only scales when it is grounded in how people actually work, requiring a strategic look at workflows across the company.' Focus shifting from individual upskilling toward 'redesigning roles, workflows and talent systems'.
note: Job and org redesign now out-ranks reskilling on the CHRO agenda. That is a demand signal for organisation design (T02.S02.P04) and workforce planning (T07.S02.P04) — both general-management topics — rather than for AI-tool training.

skill: CHRO 2026 agenda
metric: 222 CHROs surveyed July 2025. Four 2026 priorities: harness AI to revolutionize HR; shape work in the human-machine era; mobilize leaders for growth in an uncertain world; address culture atrophy to power performance. Only 47% of surveyed CHROs said their culture currently drives employee performance. 'HR must equip managers to have actionable productivity discussions with employees.'
note: Note the shift: in the 2024 survey Gartner reported leader and manager development as the #1 HR priority for the third consecutive year; for 2026 it has been reframed as 'mobilize leaders for growth' and AI value has moved to the top. Manager development has not disappeared, it has been re-labelled — worth checking the full report before quoting the ranking as a decline.

skill: Job postings shift — routine roles down, analytical and creative up
source: Harvard Business Review / HBS Working Knowledge (Ana Elena Azpurua; research assoc. with Suraj Srinivasan)
metric: 'Openings for routine, automation-prone roles fell 13% after ChatGPT's debut' while 'demand for more analytical, technical, and creative jobs grew 20%.' Analysis examined nearly all U.S. job postings from 2019 through March 2025. 'Generative AI is reshaping, not uniformly erasing, white-collar work.'
note: Behavioural evidence (postings), not stated intent — the strongest grade in this file. Caveat: the HBR write-up does not break the 20% out by seniority or separate judgment-intensive from technical roles, so do NOT cite this as 'demand for judgment grew 20%'. It is analytical + technical + creative combined.

skill: Judgment under uncertainty and sense-making as the remaining human edge
source: MIT Sloan Management Review — 'What's Your Edge? Rethinking Expertise in the Age of AI'
metric: Four domains where humans retain value: framing and question-asking ('the most valuable human expertise increasingly lies in identifying unasked questions and recognizing that there are unknown unknowns'); judgment under uncertainty ('Leaders aren't paid because they can access information; they're paid to make decisions when the stakes are real and the outcomes are uncertain'); accountability; and sense-making across domains — 'synthesize information across domains, and make creative connections that algorithms can't.'
note: Expert argument, not data — grade accordingly. But it gives ISB precise language for repositioning existing decision-making, critical-thinking and strategic-thinking courses as AI-era courses without changing the content. Could not confirm author names or exact issue date from the page.

skill: AI erodes the judgment and expertise it substitutes for
source: Harvard Business Review — Graham Kenny and Ganna Pogrebna
metric: Organisations risk becoming 'more automated, yet less adaptive; more data-driven, yet less wise.' Three risks: skill degradation as employees rely on AI rather than developing judgment and expertise; decision-making opacity as decisions become buried in opaque systems; weakened collaboration as trust-building social interaction deteriorates. Recommends protecting critical human skills, preserving transparent decision-making structures, and deliberately rebuilding collaborative spaces.
note: No quantitative evidence — conceptual only. Recorded because the deskilling argument is the mechanism by which classic capabilities become SCARCER and therefore more valuable. This is the thesis ISB needs but it is not yet evidenced; treat as a hypothesis to test, not a claim to sell.

skill: Trust as the precondition for AI value
metric: 4,000+ executives across 21 industries and 28 countries (Oct-Dec 2024). '77% of executives believe the true benefits of AI will only be possible when built on a foundation of trust.' '81% agree that trust strategy must evolve in parallel with any technology strategy.' 80% identify ensuring positive people-AI relationships as a key priority for leaders.
note: Vendor research with a consulting sale attached — discount accordingly. Useful only as corroboration that 'trust strategy' has entered the C-suite vocabulary as a named leadership responsibility.

skill: India GCC leadership pipeline gap
source: Business of GCC — GCC Talent Strategy 2026
metric: 'Senior leadership roles in GCCs are disproportionately filled through external hiring rather than internal promotion, which signals that the pipeline is not being built.' 'Mid-level managers often lack experience in global communication, executive presence, and navigating matrix organisations.' 'India's GCC ecosystem has built world-class technical depth... What it has not yet produced at scale is a pipeline of leaders who can manage global stakeholders.'
note: Qualitative trade analysis, no numbers — weak evidence, but it names exactly the ISB portfolio: executive presence (T14.S01.P01), cross-cultural communication (T14.S01.P06), matrix influence (T07.S04.P05), general management (T15.S01.P01). Worth commissioning a harder India GCC data source before using.

skill: Skill stacking over specialisation — India
source: LinkedIn Skills on the Rise 2026 (via Storyboard18)
metric: Top rising skills in India: prompt engineering, workflow automation, LLMOps, AutoML, API integration. 38% of Indian job seekers feel unprepared for technology-driven skill changes; 74% of Indian recruiters report difficulty finding qualified talent; 46% of recruiters globally rely on skills data for hiring. LinkedIn career expert Nirajita Banerjee: 'The candidates getting noticed today aren't just specialists, they're skill stackers.' People and leadership capabilities — collaboration, team management, stakeholder management — are expanding across nearly all organisational functions.
note: CONTRADICTS the human-skills thesis for India at the individual level: India's top five rising skills are all technical. The leadership-skills claim in the same report is qualitative and unranked. Honest reading: in India, AI tooling skills are what get you HIRED; leadership skills are what the employers say they can't find. Different buyers, different products.

skill: Human/leadership skills as the AI-resistant half of the résumé
source: Inc. reporting on LinkedIn Skills on the Rise 2026
metric: Fastest-growing human-centred skills identified: executive communications, leadership influence, cross-functional collaboration, relationship-building, navigating complex situations, and translating strategy into action across teams and markets. 'Companies are searching specifically for the skills AI lacks, including relationship-building, navigating complex situations, and translating strategy into action.'
note: Secondary reporting on a primary source I could not open — no percentages or ranking available, so treat as directional. 'Translating strategy into action' and 'executive communications' map cleanly to T02.S02.P01 and T14.S01.P03/P05.
